Paragraph: Thus came to pass the fateful day of Rama's exile, the dreadful realisation of which left Dasaratha devastated. He stood rooted to the ground as he gazed longingly, in the direction in which Rama had gone. So long as the dust raised by the chariot was visible that long did the king look, and when he could no longer see Rama he fell into a dead faint. Kausalya and Kaikeyi rushed to his side. Regaining his senses Dasaratha grew irate as he burst out, "Kaikeyi! Do not touch me! You are no longer my consort. I disown all relationship with you; protecting your own interests you have brought my authority to naught. The holy pact of matrimony I had entered into I now renounce, in this world and the next. If Bharata is pleased with the crown of Kosala, may his funeral offerings at my obsequies not reach me! I see the hoof marks of those magnificent horses that bore my son away, but I do not see my son". With that Dasaratha fell silent.He was shrouded in a sorrow which haunted him from the day Kaikeyi had shattered his most cherished desire of crowning Rama.
Situation/Problem_Faced: King Dasaratha is utterly devastated by Rama's departure for exile. His overwhelming sorrow and the shock of the event lead to a physical collapse (fainting). Upon regaining consciousness, his grief turns to intense anger and rejection towards Kaikeyi, whom he blames for his misfortune, expressing a profound sense of betrayal and despair over the shattered dream of crowning Rama.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage highlights the destructive power of unfulfilled desires and the profound impact of betrayal on emotional well-being. Dasaratha's extreme reaction – fainting, intense anger, and renunciation of his marriage – demonstrates the depth of his emotional distress and his inability to cope with the loss of Rama and the perceived treachery of Kaikeyi. His curse regarding Bharata's funeral offerings further underscores his bitterness and hopelessness. The lingering 'sorrow which haunted him' indicates a long-term psychological burden.
Outcome/Resolution: Dasaratha is consumed by sorrow and anger. He completely disowns Kaikeyi and expresses a curse towards Bharata, indicating his profound and lasting emotional breakdown. The final lines suggest a state of perpetual grief that has been haunting him since the initial demand for Rama's exile.
Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Dasaratha's spiritual crisis is evident in his renunciation of the 'holy pact of matrimony' and his curse upon Bharata regarding funeral offerings, reflecting a profound sense of spiritual betrayal and despair. His suffering can be seen through the lens of **Moha**, his intense attachment to Rama leading to immense sorrow when that attachment is severed. The unfolding events are a harsh **Karma Vipaka**, where past actions, even if noble in intent, lead to devastating consequences, pushing him into a deep state of **Shoka**.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Dasaratha's reaction is an intense portrayal of grief and emotional dysregulation. His initial 'devastation' and fainting are acute stress responses to shock and loss. The subsequent 'irate' outburst and complete renunciation of Kaikeyi signify profound anger, betrayal, and a breakdown in his ability to cope. His declaration that he disowns all relationship and his curse on Bharata highlight extreme feelings of hopelessness and the complete shattering of his familial bonds. The 'sorrow which haunted him' indicates a chronic, debilitating low mood and sadness, suggesting a state of psychological distress that predates this moment and now intensifies to a breaking point, culminating in a severe relationship challenge with Kaikeyi.
